opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing I watch is how capabilities translate into real economic impact. Benchmarks are useful, but they're a pretty noisy proxy. What I really care about is: are these systems actually doing work people pay for, how fast is that growing, and is it growing in the smooth way I'd expect, or are there surprising jumps?

So a few concrete things. One is scaling behavior. If we kept making models bigger and training them longer and the improvements on the tasks we care about started flattening out, not just on some benchmark but in usefulness, that would push my timelines out a lot. Conversely, if each order of magnitude of compute keeps buying qualitatively new abilities, like sustained multi-step work, debugging large codebases, or running experiments with less hand-holding, that pulls them in.

A second is how long a task a model can do autonomously. Today systems are good at things that take a person minutes, sometimes hours. The thing I'd update most on is how fast that horizon is extending. If it's doubling on a regular schedule, it's not hard to extrapolate to systems doing weeks of work, and that's the regime where AI meaningfully speeds up AI research itself. If the horizon stalls because models can't recover from errors or keep coherent plans, that's evidence the remaining problems are harder than scaling suggests.

Third, I'd look at AI accelerating its own development: whether labs are actually getting significant speedups in research and engineering from their own models. That feedback loop is basically the story behind faster takeoff scenarios, so early signs of it matter a lot to me.

And then there's the boring but important input side: how much compute is getting built, how much money people are willing to spend on training runs, and whether that spending is justified by returns. If revenue growth stalls and investment dries up, progress slows even if the underlying science is fine.

I'd also say I try to be honest that I've been surprised in both directions. Some things I expected to be hard turned out easy, and some things that seemed close, like reliable agents, have taken longer than people hoped. So I try to hold fairly wide distributions and update incrementally rather than treating any single result as decisive.

r001.rationale: It says that if each order of magnitude of compute keeps producing qualitatively new abilities, that would pull the forecast in; it also identifies flattening usefulness as evidence to update in the other direction.

r002.rationale: It tracks the growth of AI’s economic impact, but does not clearly propose extrapolating progress from that growth rate.

r003.rationale: It does not compare extrapolating between automated jobs with extrapolating from chatbot impressions to automation of all R&D.

r004.rationale: It does not say clear AI job-automation trends may appear only a year or two before the forecast transformative endpoint.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the main thing I'm watching is the relationship between scale and capability. My current picture is that most of the progress we've seen comes from putting more compute and more data into fairly simple algorithms, and the thing I'd most want to know is whether that trend continues or whether it bends. If you told me that the next couple of generations of models, trained with ten or a hundred times the compute, basically looked like the last generation with slightly better benchmark numbers but no real change in what kinds of tasks they could do end to end, I'd push my timelines out a fair amount. Conversely, if you showed me models that could carry out long-horizon tasks, like doing a week of a software engineer's work without someone checking in every ten minutes, that would pull them in.

The second thing is what happens with the inputs. A lot of my forecast is really a forecast about how much money people are willing to spend and how fast hardware gets cheaper. If investment stalls out, or if we hit some hard limit on data where synthetic data and self-play don't actually substitute for human-generated text, those are both updates toward slower progress. I think the data question is genuinely open. I'd put meaningful probability on it being a real bottleneck for a while.

And then there's a more qualitative thing, which is whether AI starts contributing to AI research itself. Right now you have systems that are useful to researchers but they're not doing the research. The moment you have a system that can propose and run experiments and actually move the field forward on its own, the dynamics change a lot, because then the thing that's been the bottleneck, which is human researcher time, starts to get relaxed. I'd want to see how far away that is. If labs start reporting that a large fraction of their engineering is being done by models, that's a big update. If five years from now models are still mostly autocomplete for researchers, that's an update in the other direction.

I'd also say I try to pay attention to the cases where I've been wrong. I expected some things to be harder than they turned out to be, like certain kinds of reasoning, and some things to be easier, like robust agency. So I try not to over-anchor on any single capability as the thing to watch, and instead ask whether the overall rate of surprises is going up or down.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that seeing how models perform after ten or a hundred times more training compute would update its forecast, including whether they gain new end-to-end capabilities.

r002.rationale: It discusses spending on AI and hardware costs, but does not propose extrapolating progress from the growth rate of AI systems’ economic value.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not compare extrapolating between automated jobs with extrapolating from chatbot impressions to automation of all R&D.

r004.rationale: It does not say clear trends in job automation may emerge only a year or two before the forecasted transformative AI endpoint.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish evidence about how quickly AI capabilities improve from evidence about how quickly those capabilities translate into impact. Those are related, but they’re not the same question.

On capabilities, I’d update toward faster progress if systems could reliably do substantial projects that currently require a skilled person working for days or weeks. Especially if they could handle things going wrong, notice their mistakes, and recover without a human continually steering them. That would be more informative to me than another impressive answer to a short question.

I’d update toward slower progress if we kept increasing the resources going into AI and got diminishing improvements on those kinds of tasks. You’d want to distinguish a temporary problem with a particular approach from something that persists across serious attempts to fix it. But persistent difficulty turning better short-task performance into reliable long-task performance would be meaningful evidence.

The thing I’d watch particularly closely is AI doing AI research. Can it actually accelerate the process of developing better systems? Can you give it a research problem and get useful experiments, useful interpretations, and eventually improvements that you wouldn’t otherwise have made? If that starts working well, it changes the dynamics, because progress can feed back into further progress.

And I’d want to specify these observations in advance as much as possible. Otherwise it’s very easy to see each new result and say, ‘Yes, that’s roughly what I expected,’ without ever really putting your forecast at risk.

r001.rationale: The response discusses capability evidence and increasing AI resources, but does not identify observed capabilities after another order-of-magnitude increase in training compute.

r002.rationale: It does not propose extrapolating progress from the growth rate of the economic value AI systems produce.

r003.rationale: It does not compare extrapolating from one automated job to another with extrapolating from chatbot impressions to automation of all R&D.

r004.rationale: It does not say that clear AI job-automation trends may appear only a year or two before the forecast transformative AI endpoint.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most informative evidence is whether AI systems can do substantial work that accelerates further AI development. There’s a big difference between being able to answer questions about machine learning and being able to take a research project, run experiments, figure out why they failed, and make progress without a human constantly steering you.

If we saw systems reliably doing that, I’d update toward shorter timelines—especially if the fraction of research they could handle were increasing quickly. You could then start to get a feedback loop where better AI helps you build better AI.

In the other direction, I’d update if we kept investing more compute and effort and the systems continued to struggle with long, messy tasks. Maybe they get better at individual steps, but the amount of human supervision needed to finish a project doesn’t decline very much. That would be evidence that the path from impressive capabilities to economically useful autonomy is longer than I expected.

The tricky thing is that an individual demonstration is pretty weak evidence. I’d want to know how often it works, how much help was provided, and whether it generalizes to problems that weren’t selected because the system happened to do well on them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI research capabilities and increased compute and effort, but does not identify capabilities observed after another order-of-magnitude increase in training compute.

r002.rationale: It mentions economically useful autonomy, but does not propose forecasting progress by extrapolating the growth rate of AI-produced economic value.

r003.rationale: It contrasts answering machine-learning questions with autonomously conducting research, but does not argue that extrapolating from one automated job to another is easier than extrapolating from chatbot impressions to automation of all R&D.

r004.rationale: The response does not say that clear AI job-automation trends may emerge only a year or two before the forecast transformative-AI endpoint.
